extracted.intended_audience: U.S. design patent applicants and IP practitioners (companies and counsel) considering international design protection
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on using the Hague Agreement international design patent application system to obtain design protection in multiple jurisdictions, including procedural differences from the PCT, examination steps, designation and fee rules, and priority timing considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designation of individual countries and payment of fees at time of filing
rubrics_metrics.description: An international design applicant must designate individual countries and pay corresponding fees at the time of filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with PCT: while a PCT applicant may select countries for national stage entry 18 months or more after the PCT filing date, Hague applicants must choose designated countries up front. Because design applicants must identify and pay for target countries at filing, applicants should identify target countries early in planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine whether target countries participate in the Hague system and file directly where necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Several countries currently do not participate in the Hague system, and applicants should determine whether they need to file a design application directly with any countries of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check the list of Hague contracting parties (examples cited: Japan, Canada, Europe). For countries not in the Hague (example: Australia and China), an applicant must file the design patent application directly with the respective national patent offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to file via the USPTO as an office of indirect filing to WIPO
rubrics_metrics.description: U.S. applicants can file with the USPTO as an office of indirect filing; the USPTO then forwards the application to WIPO for further processing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This procedural similarity to the PCT can streamline filing logistics for U.S. applicants who wish to use a centralized international route.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-step examination process under the Hague system
rubrics_metrics.description: In the Hague system, examination proceeds in a two-step process: (1) the International Bureau of WIPO conducts an initial review to confirm that formal requirements are met, and the design is then registered and published in the International Register; (2) the patent offices of the designated countries commence substantive examination according to their respective national patent laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that some designated countries do not require substantive examination, in which case the international registration becomes effective nationally. Applicants should anticipate both the WIPO formal review and later national procedures and timelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority deadline for claiming benefit is six months for design applications
rubrics_metrics.description: International design applications must be filed within six months of an earlier filed application in order to claim benefit of priority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is shorter than the utility/PCT priority period: PCT applicants can claim priority to an application filed within one year of the PCT filing date. The six-month window for designs affects timing and planning for priority claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hague system can streamline procedures and reduce overall costs for multi-jurisdictional design protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Filing an international design patent application may help to streamline administrative procedures and reduce overall costs for applicants seeking design patent protection in a number of countries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given the need to choose designated countries at the time of filing and the shorter priority window, applicants should consider whether to file internationally early on in the planning process to take advantage of potential cost and administrative efficiencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of Hague contracting parties (including EU community design coverage)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Hague contracting parties include Japan, Canada, and Europe (all 28 members of the EU via a community design registration, as well as individual European countries including non-EU members like Switzerland).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of a community design registration can cover all EU members at once under the Hague system, but verify coverage for particular countries and whether additional national filings are required for non-contracting jurisdictions.
